attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack essay, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: The normalisation keeps the chess scope and the 'despite massive data' qualifier. It is a present-tense categorical observation.

contract.note: The plain reading follows Marcus's own definition of a chess world model, which includes board state and history. Whether small chess-specialised models count as 'LLMs' is unsettled, and that choice decides the result.

evidence.note: Karvonen (COLM 2024): a chess-trained GPT learned board representations (99.6% probe accuracy, 99.8% legal moves), and interventions show it uses them causally. It is a small specialised model, and history tracking is not shown.
Acher, May 2025: most o3/o4-mini games ended in clear illegal moves, which shows behavioural unreliability. There is no representation study and no data on chess-training volume.

reviews.rationale: General-purpose reasoning models fail behaviourally (e2). But a chess-trained language model shows a learned board representation that it uses causally (e1). Whether that model is in scope, and whether it meets the history and robustness standard, is unsettled, so neither the support nor the contradiction condition is clearly met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: 'Often', 'by the midgame', declining quality and illegal moves are all preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'often' as a recurring pattern, not every game, is fair. It is ordinary to assess legality and move quality separately.

evidence.note: o3/o4-mini games mostly ended in illegal moves, with medians around 15 to 24 moves. That supports recurring illegal play by about the middlegame. There is no phase-by-phase quality comparison, and some counts are inconsistent.
In 2023, gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct played long games with only 0.3% illegal moves. That limits generalisation across LLMs, but one model does not refute 'often'.

reviews.rationale: The illegal-move part has some support for o3/o4-mini (e1), with a notable exception in gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct (e2). No evidence gives an engine-scored decline in move quality from opening to middlegame, or the phase of first illegal moves. The support condition requires both parts, so the packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own essay.

semantics.note: 'But they don't' is a categorical present-tense observation about LLMs. The normalisation matches it.

contract.note: The standard of a 'proper' model, and whether small domain-trained transformers count as LLMs, are not supplied by the speaker. The result depends on those choices.

evidence.note: Vafa et al.: transformers that navigate well still have incoherent underlying maps and are fragile under detours. This fits the claim for the tested settings.

Karvonen: a chess GPT learned a board representation that interventions show it uses causally (up to 92% success). This is strong counterevidence beyond Othello, but its scope and completeness are unsettled.
Shows a static spatial representation in Llama and explicitly excludes movement and dynamics. It does not meet the dynamic-model standard.

reviews.rationale: The evidence points both ways. Navigation models show incoherent world models (e1). A chess-trained transformer shows an emergent board representation that it uses causally (e2), which may meet the contradiction condition if small domain models count and partial completeness is enough. Those scope and standard questions are unsettled, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his essay.

semantics.note: The two-part claim is preserved: ChatGPT uses factual information unreliably, and it lacks an explicit, stable internal model.

contract.note: The plain reading separates the reliability part from the representation part. 'Reliability' as ordinarily dependable answers is a fair standard.

evidence.note: OpenAI system card (company disclosure): PersonQA hallucination rates of 33% for o3 and 48% for o4-mini on facts about people. This supports the unreliability part, but says nothing about internal representations.
The launch post confirms o3 and o4-mini were available in ChatGPT before the essay. It does not identify which model produced Marcus's example.

reviews.rationale: The factual-unreliability part has support from the PersonQA hallucination rates in ChatGPT-available models (e1). No evidence addresses whether ChatGPT has an explicit, stable internal model, and the support condition requires direct evidence for that part. The claim as a whole is not settled.
